Not a bad game, otherwise I would have refunded (or never bought, given there's a demo). It just feels like a lot of missed opportunity and didn't seem to reward the time put into it. You start off a run by shooting a die and it bumps around and combines a few times. If you're lucky it combines maybe 10 times. If you're really lucky, you can get like 20 combines or something but that almost never happens. 20 minutes later, you're at the end of the run and... it's exactly the same situation. Why didn't they lean into the concept and have like 100 dice bouncing around, combining, exploding, triggering big effects, doing crazy stuff? Why not have more stuff on the board itself, affecting the path of the dice? Why not have crazier effects instead of "deal damage" and "deal 1.5x damage" and "deal 2x damage"? It just feels so incredibly lame compared to the concept's potential. And then the choices you make during the run are incredibly minimal. Would you rather take a new die, heal 9, or take a one-time consumable that... heals 9? Cool. The first few hours promise something more and it's somewhat addictive at first but then you just realize there's nothing really happening.

TLDR: there's a lot of effort put into this game, but the gameplay itself just isn't executed that well. Why dice? Like, this is gonna sound nitpicky at first, but bear with me. Why build an aesthetic around dice, if you aren't actually using it? You don't roll the dice, the random numbers of the dice don't come into play, so why make it dice? You're shooting an object at other objects, sometimes merging, sometimes bouncing off to merge with other things, so why not marbles? The central theme of this game doesn't actually apply to the gameplay. The physics of the game also feels weird. I don't actually know if the models of the dice are cubes in engine, but it's really weird to have this intent of using physics to bounce dice around and make plays but merging dice prevents you from making a lot of plays like that. The dice aren't launched with enough velocity to push other dice around in a satisfying way, their shapes aren't really conducive for that, merging them combines two dice but then launches that dice into the air to fly towards the nearest dice of that same value which also eliminates a lot of strategy to the game.

The game fills the void left by 100%ing Peglin... but misses the mark in a big way. It's really sad, because it's a game let down by what feels like a *single* point of misunderstanding of the game's offered experience amongst the developers. The core gameplay loop of Rune Dice is shooting dice to create merges and as your emrge more dice you get more damage; so it follows naturally that the shooting of the dice should be the thing that you upgrade and get better at through the run. Different dice effects, different dice values - those are there... but ths hooting of the dice? How the dice interact? How they jump? What they seek out? Nothing - or close to it. This means that even as your runs get stronger you don't *have more fun*. The game plays identically at the beginning as it does at the end, and this is so, so, so, so, so, so big an oversight that playing it feels like staring at the mona lisa without the details on her face filled in, or like watching a movie where only the sound file for the music is playing, no voices. It's heartbreaking and would have taken exactly one smart person to point out when they made their first vertical slice.

The fact there are dice involved is almost meaningless as I think all sides are identical, but they do still make for a fun billiards like gameplay sliding cubes in such a way to try to get giant chain reactions and a fun "deckbuilder" as you decide which special dice you add to your dice sack.

Another of those games, just like Peglin, where you keep watching yourself taking damage constantly from ranged attacks, without any way to defend yourself (not every character has shield dice...) Because of that, you have to keep healing yourself after each fight, effectively ignoring all upgrades. Having to always facetank isn't fun to me at all. Also, overall balancing isn't great, bomb dice are really op. Shields are also op (how ironic), as you can stall the fight to grind money. And the most frustrating: your runs will end, right when the interesting aspect of building a dice deck finally starts to show.

This game is the most fun I had playing roguelites in recent years. Cool idea, short runs that don't consume your time (with longer runs planned to be added in the future), a bunch of different dice, runes and relics to keep runs fresh and feeling different. Every class feels unique and there's a bit of strategy in choosing the right class for the right map even if every class can beat every boss. I had this game on my wishlist for quite some time and I actually ended up receiving a review key for it, the fact that I have a 100% achievements and I still want to keep playing has to mean something. Plus for the low price it's being offered it doesn't matter if you are a casual player, achievement hunter or true completionist you will get your money's worth. AND DON'T FORGET DEVS HAVE ANNOUNCED MORE UPDATES WITH MORE CONTENT ARE COMING.

It's like 60% of a Game. It's kind of fun and novel for a while, but after you've done about 10 runs and played with a couple of classes, it just fades, feels flat, and unsatisfying. Right now I was playing to finally unlock Archer, which is locked behind an astronomically high, very specific requirement, so I was trying over multiple days to play a certain way, but it never worked, and it always ended with a: "Why am I playing this? I'm bored." and quit. I don't know how often I'll be coming back, but I don't think it's a lot. It looks nice and is fun when it's novel, but you've extremely quickly seen everything this game has to offer, and compared to deckbuilders with a lot of depth and complexity, this game is severely lacking. So if you're swimming in money and want to distract yourself from your mortal coil for an hour or two, go for it, but if you want something to sink your teeth and hours into, this isn't it.

Update: After I played many runs in Classic run, I've changed my positive review to negative. The idea could've been nice, but in reality it'll show you the ugliest sides of the game, especially to bonkers RNG with dice bounces and rewards. It took me 8,4 hours to beat all the bosses on hard in the normal run (and also I acquired 85% of the achievements), but I could finish the beat the classic run with each character achievement only after 24,3 hours. Personally I love the game, but I think it’s an extremely niche game. After deeper look into who may I recommend it I got the conclusion that I can’t really pinpoint any group. I think only people who approach this game very lightheartedly will find enjoyment. The people who are looking for a 30 minutes fun, where the game can end in defeat, because RNG wasn’t in favor of you. I like Rune Dice, because it’s a quick, fun, RNG game for me. I basically try to do the same thing all the time, but the game will throw random challenges at me. I don’t mind losses, I’m used to the unexpected elements of Rune Dice. That’s being said I’m not 100% happy, just the positives outweighs the negative elements. The dice bouncing physics is funky, many times the target selection for merge is illogical. I play on 2x speed, but I think I’ll enjoy on 4x more. Dice upgrade altars show 70% chance to succeed, but it feels more like 50% on hard difficulty. Even though there are 3 biomes with different type of enemies, but the setup is picked from a limited pool of variations. Ranged units will be always in the back, there aren’t any random orders. Even with the relic or the rune the order of the units won’t be mixed up that much most of the time. To beat the more gimmicky bosses you’ll need specific relics. It’s really up to RN Jesus if you’ll have them in the store after several refreshes. I would say the biggest misleading parts are the tags in the Steam store. Everything is true in some degree. Deckbuilding is limited mostly to the dice, but everything is just RNG. You can’t really execute your plan to get the right dice and relics, it would be up to the game if you’ll have the chance to acquire them. I don’t see any RPG element beyond the relics. You can’t really customize your character, there aren’t any attributes or level ups. There isn’t any dialog system. Strategy is a big offender. I think your most strategic decisions are which character you choose and on the randomly generated map which paths you take. Dice, relics, enemies are random, dice physics and paths are wonky, tactical at best. Roguelike and roguelite should mean that with experience you can further progress, but in Rune Dice the learning curve is extremely short and it isn’t steep. Here the tags mean that your play will be random and somewhat unique all the time.

The music is a bop, the visuals are great. The animations are cute and the sounds do what you want them to do. The game is responsive, the dopamine is there, and the unlocks are paced well and provide a solid sense of progression. Game is fun for a short time but flawed. I will continue to play in hopes that the last unlock I have my eye on shifts things. You need to know I have played on hard mode for about 6 of my almost 10 hours and switched to easy for a few hours to see that all problems are equally present in both. I have a full library and have never considered a game too hard- them's the breaks with roguelites. I'm saying all of that because it will be easy to read some of what's coming up as 'this game is too hard.' That is not the complaint. This game lacks a strong sense of agency after the character selection screen, so I do not feel I lost or won because the game is hard or easy, I lost or won because I was always going to, based on scatter positions. There is some agency, but not much. When the game is 'hard', I am not convinced it was beatable based on what unlocks are available. It is very easy to be put in an unwinnable position. Bigger complaint first, this isn't a dice game, so the marketing is fairly deceptive, but in fairness in promo images if you somehow already know to look closely you will see the issue. There are numbered cubes but they all have the same identical face (a 5 only has 5's, a 3 only has 3s, with no variance I have found in hours of playing). The only real variance is the specific way they are scattered, and your plan is to knock them around billiards style to optimize around the fact that when two matching numbers meet, they merge into the next number and jump towards a cube already showing that number (just look at the marketing gif's and notice each dice only has one face and you'll get how it plays pretty quickly). Face variance for RNG is the point of dice so I can't stress what a marketing mismatch it is. Find me another dice game where the dice is the same on all sides, and I will bet that it does not market itself on being dice-focused. This is a real-time physics based merge game. Call it Rune Merge or something. Some enemies are designed pretty poorly and turn off or nullify what little agency you have. The sand blocks are a massive problem. There is also absolutely no way to play around a creature gaining thorn damage, you just have to hope you haven't damaged it that many times, but your control over the order of the cubes and how they are applied feels like 80% pre-ordained, and ranged enemies will be putting damage on you every turn or every other turn, and the board re-sets after a few throws, so you do not have the luxury of slow-playing on purpose to only hit the enemy with big cubes (the only organically occurring alternative to just deciding to stop attacking and die, for what your board is likely to look like at that point). I've lost runs to a creature that just dealt 6 damage to me every time I dealt 1 damage to it. I had to deal 1 damage to it multiple times to be able to deal 2, then 3, etc. You get 49 health and I spent 24 of mine dealing 6 damage to one giant enemy supporting a boss. Enemies that place their own cubes seem to always place them on the 'frontlines' soaking up a majority of your sightlines so that you don't even feel like you can play around them- you just have to suck it up and hit them to power through constant ranged damage. To give the players agency, there needs to be some way to nudge the table. There are one-off 'dice' that are not rolled or scattered at all but are just clicked on and dragged that do a fairly watered-down version of this, but choosing one always costs a long-term benefit and it is single-use for the entire run. You will give up the chance for another cube, or a cube upgrade, to be able to push some dice together or apart in a small circle a single time. It is not enough for the price you pay. The tone of the whole game mechanically winds up being, "You do not have a choice unless you're intentionally playing badly to feel like you do, by 'choosing' to make failing gambits". The frequency of shop-manipulating items is way too high for a game where you might visit the shop a gluttonous ("choosing to lose") three times during a run max. There is not enough gold or enough shop opportunities for them to ever feel like they paid off. Two things I am still unsure if I am imagining. One is still being tested but the other I just cannot come to heads or tails on. It feels like the higher a dice gets, the less it is willing to travel to join up with its mate. I have had 4's and higher even seem to bounce off each other. If this is in my imagination then there's nothing they can do about that, but if 5's and 6's are limping along by design then this is the closest I've ever come to a 'ruined climax' mechanic in a videogame. Like I said, I will continue playing for a bit to find more of what I like, but the issues are just rough to play around.

I know that it's part of the deal when playing a roguelite, but I still feel like the amount of random is just too high in this one. I'm usually one to scrunch my face when a reviewer says a game has too much luck, assuming they're probably just not great at the game, or that the luck is still otherwise appropriate once settled in. But on most runs of Rune Dice I feel like I really don't have anything to change for my next run. This [b][i]could[/i][/b] be fine in a roguelite, because a core positive of the subgenre is that you can count on little upgrades between runs to help you make meta progress as you go. But in this case it takes so long to level, and then has so little advantage. But worse and more importantly, the levels cap out too soon in my opinion. Another little idiosyncrasy is that while the game signals that higher numbers are better, they often aren't. Level up for higher numbered starting dice (which are mandatory). Spend much more gold for the higher numbered dice mid-run. "Upgrade" is the word used to raise the number on a die in your deck. Risk for higher dice at the threat of deleted dice in the magic circle spots. And yet, here you are with no way to combo lest you keep those boys low. Maybe that's just me, but it feels like sometimes the language of the game is trying to trick players into engaging in entire systems at their peril. You should be ignoring shiny things, silly. Just hold onto those boring blank white 1's. Just press "skip" when you get a reward. I'll choose "recommend" because if you play the game in just the right moderation with just the right amount of casual energy it works fine. If you start getting sweaty and frustrated though, it means it's time to try something that might support that intensity and precision.

I really enjoyed dice rune, lovely pixel art, fun music and an addictive gameplay that was great to zone out to. I quite easily stacked up the hours on this one, but I do have some thoughts. The sense of strategizing and player agency doesn't *really* come from the dice "battles" but instead the room/item/dice pick up choice & even then you options are quite limited. For a lot of runs, I found this to create a relaxing almost casual gaming experience, which was what I needed at the time. However due to the dice rolling side of things being so straight forward, after 30+ hours I started to wish for more dimension to the game play. Character abilities (not just special dice), new items/ methods to manipulate the die rolling zone, different sided dice? etc stuff like that Keep in mind, I only started to want more as I played more. If you're looking for a fun, engaging game to use for around 15-20 hours. I don't think you can go wrong with Dice Rune. I just think it has the potential to be more re-playable/ addictive, like other traditional-gaming inspired pixel games.

This game has a lot going for it that I like and I will continue to play it. Art, strategy, pacing, rogueish-ness loop, all good. The dice physics can be very frustrating at times though. There is a learning curve, but there is also a lot of unpredictability and chaos that some how makes the system feel more random than if you were actually rolling the dice for a result. A bad distribution of dice can have devastating consequences and there's only so much it feels like you can do to control those factors. I think it would benefit from a training mode or a feature that better outlines what dice are going to be contacted at the end of the path and what direction those dice struck are going to go after contact. Something of a very short-ranged "gimmie" system would be nice as well. Since there's only so much you can do with aiming, having two dice that should merge come with in a hairs breath of each other or landing almost touching is very defeating. Maybe I need to progress further and unlock these features, but they feel like they are beginner friendly ways to train up or just enjoy more casually. I really enjoy classic mode. I would love to see a similar system but with a straight billiards theme.
